content: Systematic screening for tuberculosis (TB) disease is recommended for adults and adolescents living with HIV. The World Health Organization (WHO) advises using a four-symptom screen that includes current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats. If any of these symptoms are reported, the individual should undergo further evaluation for TB and other diseases. This recommendation is supported by strong evidence with moderate certainty. For children under 10 years of age living with HIV, systematic TB screening should include symptoms such as current cough, fever, poor weight gain, or close contact with a person diagnosed with TB. This recommendation is also strong but based on low-certainty evidence regarding test accuracy. C-reactive protein (CRP) testing with a threshold of >5 mg/L may be used to screen for TB in adults and adolescents living with HIV. This is a conditional recommendation supported by low-certainty evidence for test accuracy. Similarly, chest X-rays may be used for TB screening in this population, with a conditional recommendation and moderate-certainty evidence. In populations where TB screening is recommended, computer-aided detection software can be used to interpret digital chest X-rays instead of human readers. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. Molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDTs) are suggested for TB screening among adults and adolescents living with HIV. These tests are conditionally recommended with moderate-certainty evidence for test accuracy. For medical inpatients with HIV in settings where TB prevalence exceeds 10%, systematic testing for TB using mWRDTs is strongly recommended, supported by moderate-certainty evidence. In 2019, an estimated 44% of people living with HIV who also had TB did not access care, and TB accounted for 30% of all HIV-related deaths. Early detection and treatment of TB among people living with HIV are therefore critical to reducing morbidity and mortality. The WHO four-symptom screen remains the simplest and most non-invasive tool for TB screening, requiring no infrastructure. However, its specificity is limited, particularly among medical inpatients with HIV in high TB prevalence settings. Programs may consider supplementing the four-symptom screen with additional tools like CRP testing or chest X-rays to improve diagnostic accuracy. CRP testing is particularly accurate among outpatients with HIV not receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART). When used after a positive four-symptom screen, CRP testing with a threshold of >5 mg/L improves specificity while maintaining sensitivity. The combination of the four-symptom screen and chest X-ray, where a positive result from either tool prompts further diagnostic confirmation, has the highest sensitivity for TB screening among outpatients receiving ART. Studies on computer-aided detection software for chest X-rays show variability in accuracy compared to human readers. Further evidence is needed to optimize the use of this technology among people living with HIV. Diagnosing TB in people living with HIV can be challenging due to atypical clinical presentations, especially in advanced disease. Bacteriological testing is essential for accurate diagnosis. Molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests are preferred as initial tests over smear microscopy or culture. These tests detect TB and rifampicin resistance and are critical for effective treatment. The lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) test is an add-on test for people living with HIV, particularly those with advanced disease. It is performed on urine samples and is part of the standard care package for advanced HIV. A positive LF-LAM test predicts mortality and, when combined with appropriate treatment, saves lives. Next-generation tests with improved sensitivity for patients with higher CD4 counts are under development. Once available, these tests may expand TB diagnostic options for people living with HIV. Molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests include products like Xpert® MTB/RIF, Xpert® Ultra, Truenat™, and others. Xpert® Ultra is more sensitive than Xpert® MTB/RIF, particularly for people living with HIV, but has slightly lower specificity due to false positives in individuals with a history of TB treatment. Moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are the latest addition to WHO-recommended diagnostic tools. These tests require laboratory infrastructure and are suitable for high-throughput settings. They detect TB and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, with some systems also capable of SARS-CoV-2 testing. WHO recommends molecular rapid diagnostic tests for diagnosing pulmonary TB and, in some cases, extrapulmonary TB. Xpert® Ultra is particularly sensitive for these populations, including children and those with extrapulmonary TB. In settings with high TB prevalence, molecular rapid diagnostic tests are recommended for screening all adults and adolescents living with HIV. Positive screening results should be followed by diagnostic assessments to avoid overtreatment. Priority should be given to using these tests as diagnostic tools before scaling them up for screening purposes.
